hints: Look at the spacing of the straight incident wavefronts compared with the width of the gap in each diagram.
Recall that diffraction is greatest when gap width is similar to wavelength $\lambda$, giving spreading into the shadow behind the barrier.
Check which transmitted pattern keeps the same $\lambda$ but changes from straight lines to near-circular arcs centred on the gap.
walkthrough: Identify the incident waves on the left as straight parallel wavefronts moving toward the barrier with a narrow gap.
State the rule for diffraction at a gap: spreading is significant when gap width is of order $\lambda$, and the transmitted fronts become curved and enter the geometric shadow.

Compare incident $\lambda$ with gap width: in B they are similar, in C the incident $\lambda$ is smaller than the gap, in A the pattern does not maintain circular spreading, and in D there is no spreading.
Require that frequency and speed, hence $\lambda$, are unchanged on transmission, so the spacing of the curved fronts after the barrier must match the incident spacing.
Only B shows near-semicircular wavefronts centred on the gap, spreading widely sideways while keeping the same spacing. This is option B.

options.A: The transmitted fronts do not spread well into the shadow region and quickly become straight, which does not show strong diffraction through a narrow gap.
options.B: The gap width is similar to the incident wavelength, so the waves spread out into near-semicircular fronts centred on the gap with unchanged wavelength.
options.C: The incident wavelength is much smaller than the gap width, so the spreading should be much less curved with a flatter central section, not strong semicircular diffraction.
options.D: The waves continue as short straight segments with no spreading into the shadow region, so no diffraction is shown.
